abstract: The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 provides one of the most comprehensive employer-survey-based assessments of labor market transformation, drawing on responses from over 1,000 employers across 55 economies. The report projects that by 2030, 92 million jobs will be displaced while 170 million new jobs will be created, yielding a net increase of 78 million positions globally. Robotics and automation are expected to drive business transformation for 58% of employers surveyed, making it the most-cited transformation driver. The report finds that while robots and automation are forecast to displace 5 million more jobs than they directly create in existing occupational categories, the broader economic effects—including new industries, increased productivity, and expanded services—generate substantial net job creation. The skills landscape is shifting rapidly, with analytical thinking, resilience, and technology literacy identified as the most important workforce competencies for the coming period.
keyFindings: 92 million jobs projected to be displaced and 170 million created by 2030, yielding a net increase of 78 million jobs globally.
58% of employers cite robotics and automation as the most important driver of business transformation.
Robots and automation forecast to displace 5 million more jobs than they directly create, but broader economic effects generate net positive job creation.
Analytical thinking, resilience, flexibility, and technology literacy are ranked as the most important skills for the 2025-2030 period.
The report reflects employer expectations from over 1,000 organizations across 55 economies, making it one of the largest forward-looking labor market surveys.
methodology: Survey of over 1,000 employers across 55 economies and 22 industry clusters, covering over 14 million workers. Employers report on expected changes in job roles, skills requirements, and workforce strategies over a five-year horizon (to 2030). Job creation and displacement estimates derived from employer-reported expectations aggregated across the global sample. Skills demand analysis based on employer rankings and job posting trend data.
qualifiers: Forward-looking survey data reflects employer expectations, which historically diverge from actual outcomes—previous WEF reports have both over- and under-estimated specific trends. The net +78 million figure depends on new job categories that may not yet exist, making it inherently speculative. Survey respondents are typically large multinational employers, whose perspectives may not represent SMEs that employ the majority of workers globally. Job creation and displacement figures are not independent estimates but rather aggregated employer projections subject to anchoring bias. The five-year time horizon (to 2030) is short enough to be plausible but long enough that significant economic shocks could alter trajectories.
